forces: Soprano, two violins, viola and cello
performers: Carmel String Quartet; Rona Israel-Kolatt, soprano
question: What connects musical phrases when a home key becomes uncertain?
intro: “I feel air from another planet”: Stefan George’s words accompany Schoenberg’s departure from a governing key. Four strings and a soprano carry the finale; the twelve-tone method is still more than a decade away.

cues.title: An unsettled opening
cues.text: Across the instrumental introduction, follow the chromatic lines without expecting an immediate home-key cadence. The movement will not avoid tonal reference altogether, but its opening suspends the usual harmonic bearings.
cues.evidence: Therese Muxeneder’s Arnold Schönberg Center account identifies the introduction’s suspended tonality. The report shows a quiet opening, but its unstable key estimates are not evidence of particular harmonies.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Air from another planet
cues.text: The poem begins “Ich fühle Luft von anderem Planeten” — “I feel air from another planet”. Across the vocal passages, follow the soprano as a melodic part among the strings rather than treating the instruments as one undifferentiated accompaniment.
cues.evidence: The words come from George’s poem as set in the score. A measured change around 1:14 suggests the first vocal span, but the sung words and entrance have not been timed.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: George’s seventh ring
cues.text: Both poems in the quartet come from Stefan George’s Der siebente Ring, published in 1907. The last two movements set “Litanei” and “Entrückung”, adding a soprano to the four string players.
cues.evidence: Muxeneder identifies the poems, collection and scoring: https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/second-string-quartet-op-10

cues.title: Independent lines
cues.text: In the more active stretches, try following one line through changes of register, then attend to another. A phrase can be connected by its shape even when the accompanying pitches do not establish a familiar key.
cues.evidence: This is a listening strategy for the score’s interacting lines. Increased recorded activity around 2:20–2:35 supports a broad placement, not identification of particular string parts.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Small shapes as landmarks
cues.text: Instead of waiting only for a familiar chord progression, follow a short melodic shape as its rhythm or register changes. Repetition and transformation can connect phrases that share no settled tonic.
cues.evidence: The Arnold Schönberg Center account describes motivic transformation and weakened tonal bearings. No particular motif entrance is assigned to this second.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A short forceful swell
cues.text: The surrounding stretch builds towards a brief crest, then withdraws. Listen to the relation between that short expansion and the quieter phrases on either side.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises markedly around 4:25–4:30 and falls again by 4:45. This measures the contour without identifying a sung syllable or instrumental entrance.

cues.title: An audience interrupts
cues.text: The Rosé Quartet and soprano Marie Gutheil-Schoder gave the Vienna premiere in December 1908. In an account written in 1936–37, Schoenberg recalled laughter beginning in the second movement and continuing through much of the two George settings.
cues.evidence: Schoenberg’s retrospective introductory note is reproduced by the Arnold Schönberg Center; it is testimony written nearly thirty years later: https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/second-string-quartet-op-10

cues.title: A surge and its retreat
cues.text: In this stretch, closely spaced attacks gather force before another withdrawal. Compare the activity inside the surge with the space it leaves afterwards.
cues.evidence: The report shows frequent attacks and high relative level around 5:20–5:25, followed by a marked retreat through 5:40. The cue concerns that surrounding span.

cues.title: Quiet does not mean still
cues.text: Listen through the quiet restart for small movements that accumulate before the sound regains weight. Reduced intensity need not stop the interaction between the lines.
cues.evidence: Relative level is very low around 5:50–5:55, then rises through 6:10 while detected attacks increase. The analysis does not separate the performers.

cues.title: Two later waves
cues.text: The later span contains a strong surge, a withdrawal and another rise. Listen across both waves rather than taking the first crest as an ending.
cues.evidence: The highest five-second relative-level window is around 7:05; a drop around 7:15 is followed by renewed strength around 7:30–7:35.

cues.title: A long closing paragraph
cues.text: The score ends with a long string-only coda after the soprano’s part is complete. As the closing span unfolds, listen for how sustained writing can continue the argument after the poem has run its course.
cues.evidence: Schoenberg describes the instrumental coda in his introductory note. The quieter, more sustained span after about 7:52 suggests its location, but the soprano’s final word is not established by the analysis.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Remembered silence in the hall
cues.text: Schoenberg’s 1936–37 account singles out the coda: after the audience had interrupted even the singer, he remembered the string-only ending proceeding without audible disturbance. This is his retrospective testimony about the 1908 premiere, not a description of this recording.
cues.evidence: The claim is explicitly attributed to Schoenberg’s introductory note, reproduced here: https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/second-string-quartet-op-10

cues.title: A recognisable destination
cues.text: The closing paragraph leads towards F♯ major. The quartet began in F♯ minor: a recognisable tonal destination remains even though much of this finale has avoided conventional routes between keys.
cues.evidence: The opening and final tonal destinations come from the score. The report’s F♯-centred closing span is compatible with that account, but its changing key labels do not identify individual chords.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The final harmony and decay
cues.text: Near the end, listen for the final major harmony and the sound remaining after it. Reaching a tonal conclusion does not turn the preceding chromatic writing into an ordinary succession of keys.
cues.evidence: The score supplies the final F♯ major. Relative level recedes around 9:50–10:00; the later rise after 10:04 is not treated as another musical event without listening review.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A fifth line enters the unsettled harmony
transitions.how: The soprano enters a texture the strings have already made unstable, rather than arriving over a newly established tonic chord. Chromatic lines and fifth-related pitch connections cross registers; the cello participates in that movement instead of supplying a dependable dominant–tonic bass. Adding the voice changes the colour and gives the phrases words, but does not replace the string argument with a tune and chordal accompaniment. Schoenberg asks for the voice to stand out by timbre, not simply by being louder.
transitions.evidence: The 1:14 section boundary marks an analysis change into the provisional first vocal span. Therese Muxeneder’s Arnold Schönberg Center account describes the introduction’s suspended tonality, fifth relationships and Schoenberg’s balance instruction. The first syllable is not aligned, and twelve-pitch coverage here is not described as twelve-tone serial technique.

transitions.title: The strings continue after the words
transitions.how: The later vocal waves subside into a long string-only coda. Removing the soprano does not restore the opening introduction: the four instruments continue working with the movement’s material after the poem has ended. Sustained lines replace the preceding forceful attacks, and F♯ increasingly becomes a point of reference. The route is not a conventional retransition waiting on C♯ dominant; tonal focus returns within the chromatic writing before the final major chord makes the destination explicit.
transitions.evidence: The 7:52 section boundary follows the later swells and a fall in level near 7:50, with few detected attacks and F♯ prominent in the closing span. Schoenberg’s introductory note, reproduced by the Arnold Schönberg Center, identifies the long instrumental coda after the soprano finishes. The span indicates that larger handover; it does not claim to time the singer’s last word.

transitions.title: Chromatic lines settle into a major triad
transitions.how: The remaining motion settles into F♯ major: F♯ in the harmonic foundation, with A♯ and C♯ completing the triad. The major third matters because the whole quartet began in F♯ minor, with A♮. Schoenberg recovers a recognisable destination without making the finale’s intervening chromatic fields into a chain of ordinary keys. Held string sound and diminishing movement let the final consonance register as an ending, not as the start of a conventional recapitulation.
transitions.evidence: The 9:50 section boundary lies in the final F♯-centred span, whose level falls through 10:00. The score and Arnold Schönberg Center commentary establish the F♯-major ending and the quartet’s original F♯ minor; the analysis alone cannot identify the major third. The later recorded activity after 10:04 is excluded from this account of the musical close.

composer.epithet: A Viennese teacher who took motivic development beyond the key signature, then made twelve notes carry the work of a tonal system.
facts: Largely self-taught; counterpoint lessons with Alexander Zemlinsky; close study of Bach, Beethoven, Brahms and Wagner
Berg and Webern from 1904 · Prussian Academy of Arts, Berlin, 1926–33 · University of California, Los Angeles, 1936–44
Developing variation · free atonality · twelve-tone composition · Sprechstimme
Painter; author of Harmonielehre (1911); founder of the Society for Private Musical Performances
composer.background:
Arnold Schoenberg was born in Vienna’s Leopoldstadt, the son of a Jewish shopkeeper, and learned the violin as a child. When his father died in 1889, the family’s finances made extended formal study impossible. He worked in a bank from 1891 to 1895, played chamber music with friends and learned composition by examining scores. Alexander Zemlinsky, whom he met through the amateur orchestra Polyhymnia, gave him counterpoint lessons. Schoenberg’s later teaching grew from this close reading: he explained, with unusual insistence, what each note in Bach, Mozart, Beethoven and Brahms was doing.

In the 1890s the apparent opposition between Brahms and Wagner organised Viennese musical argument. Schoenberg took techniques from both. From Brahms came the continuous alteration of a small motif, later described as developing variation; from Wagner came chromatic harmony whose resolution could be postponed across an entire scene. Verklärte Nacht, written in 1899 for string sextet, applies these procedures to Richard Dehmel’s poem about a woman confessing to her lover that she carries another man’s child. The opening D minor eventually transforms into D major, supplying the work’s large-scale harmonic argument.
